title: U.S. sports executive buys minority stake in second-tier Bolton after Donald Trump pardon
content:
A high-profile U.S. sports executive pardoned by Donald Trump in December, following an indictment for allegedly rigging a bidding process, has bought a minority stake in Championship club Bolton Wanderers.

Tim Leiweke was accused by the Department of Justice last summer of orchestrating a conspiracy to put off a rival bid for the construction of a sports arena at the University of Texas so that his own company, Oak View Group (OVG), could win the $375million contract.

In the wake of the indictment, Leiweke stepped down as OVG’s chief executive and the company agreed to pay $15m in penalties for its part in the arena scheme. But, six months later, while DoJ antitrust lawyers were preparing their case against him, Leiweke was quietly pardoned by Trump, with no explanation as to why he was shutting the corruption case down.

The following day, Leiweke gave a statement to the Sports Business Journal that said he did not “have the words to adequately convey my profound gratitude to President Trump”, before adding that the pardon had given him and his family “a new lease on life with which we will be grateful and good stewards”.

Leiweke has wasted little time on delivering on that promise. In May, the 69-year-old invested €100million ($114m; £85m) in newly-promoted Serie A side Venezia, with his daughter Francesca Bodie becoming the club’s president. Last month, he was blocked from buying a 16 per cent stake Benfica, as the Portuguese club’s board raised concerns about being part of a multi-club group.

And now Leiweke, his daughter and former OVG executive Keegan McDonald have formed a new entity called Entrepreneur Equity Partners to buy a stake in Bolton, who were promoted back to English football’s second tier via the play-offs last season.

As part of the investment, Leiweke will join the board, with McDonald becoming a board observer. They will sit alongside the majority-shareholder Nick Luckock and fellow minority shareholders Sharon Brittan, the club’s chair, and Michael James.

Brittan, James and Luckock, under the guise of Football Ventures, rescued the former Premier League side from bankruptcy in 2019 and have guided the club back from League Two, the fourth tier, to the Championship.

“I have always believed that reaching the Championship would not be the end of our journey but the point at which we looked for the right partners to help us solidify our position there,” said Brittan in a statement published on the club website on Friday. “In EEP, we have found a partner who understands our town, our community and the way we do things, who shares our vision for the future and brings real, proven experience of successfully building clubs and bringing supporters closer to the team.”

While some fans may have some misgivings about Leiweke’s recent legal issues, his investment in Bolton was approved by the new Independent Football Regulator, and he is experienced in professional sports.

A long-time associate of billionaire businessman Philip Anschutz, Leiweke was president of Anschutz Entertainment Group (AEG) between 1996 and 2013. At the time, AEG owned the NHL’s Los Angeles Kings, MLS side Los Angeles Galaxy and a stake in the NBA’s Lakers, as well several arenas, including the O2 in London.

He then spent two years in charge of Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment, the owner of Toronto’s NBA, NHL and MLS franchises, before founding OVG in 2015. The company manages numerous sports venues around the world, including several that it has built.

In the press release that announced the Bolton deal, Leiweke said he and his EEP partners were at Wembley to witness the team’s promotion “and the support we saw from the fans that day told us everything we needed to know” about the club and its fanbase.

“We are here to honour that legacy and those supporters and take this club to the next level,” he added. “We will be bringing the best of what we have learnt as partners to many leading global teams to make Bolton Wanderers stronger than ever before. We are proud to join at this stage of this club’s incredible journey.”

Neither he nor the club, however, mentioned the pardon, without which this deal would have very likely been blocked.

When asked if the pardon was the crucial factor in approving Leiweke, the IFR told The Athletic it does not comment on its Owners, Directors and Senior Executives test assessments but explained that its final decisions are published on its website.

The Athletic has approached Bolton and Leiweke for comment.
